subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Four Angles at a Crossing: Spotting the Pattern

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw two lines on a plain sheet that intersect. Measure the four angles with a protractor. Repeat for four such pairs. Observe patterns among the angles and reason whether vertically opposite angles are always equal.
In Fig. 5.2, if ∠a is 120°, figure out the measurements of ∠b, ∠c, and ∠d without drawing and measuring them.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: List all linear pairs and pairs of vertically opposite angles in Fig. 5.3 (two intersecting lines forming angles a, b, c, d).

homework.description: Can two straight lines intersect at more than one point?

time_bands.activity: Students draw two intersecting lines on plain paper, label the four angles a, b, c, d, and measure each with a protractor. Activity 1, p.107 ("draw two lines on a plain sheet that intersect....") anchors this opening — students complete all four repetitions and record their angle measurements in a table.

Class pools measurements on the board. Students identify that opposite angle pairs share the same measure across all their drawings, prompting the vocabulary: linear pair (angles summing to 180°) and vertically opposite angles (equal angles across the intersection). The 'Measurements and Geometry' note is read aloud to distinguish measured approximations from exact geometric reasoning.

Figure it Out, section 5.1 p.107 ("In Fig. 5.2, if ∠a is 120°, figure out the measurements....") is attempted individually, then shared. Students explain their reasoning using the linear-pair relationship, not their rulers. Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108 ("List all linear pairs and pairs of vertically opposite angles....") follows as paired work, reinforcing naming.

Whole-class debrief: teacher elicits the two key facts — adjacent angles at an intersection sum to 180°, and opposite angles are equal — using students' own words. Students record both facts in their notebooks with a labelled diagram of their own.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who list all four angles as 'vertically opposite' rather than just the two opposite pairs; naming them aloud while pointing to the diagram usually corrects this quickly. The 'Measurements and Geometry' interlude is worth a brief class read — it signals that small discrepancies in measured values are expected, not errors.

periods.activity_title: Proving Vertical Angles Equal — No Protractor Needed

textbook_items_in_class.description: What patterns do you observe among the four angles formed when two lines intersect (after Activity 1)?
Is it always true that vertically opposite angles are equal for any pair of intersecting lines? Check for different measures of ∠a and reason whether the property holds generally.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the angle table from their earlier measurements. Figure it Out, section 5.1 p.107 ("What patterns do you observe among the four angles formed when two lines intersect....") is posed as a whole-class question; students articulate the linear-pair and vertically-opposite patterns in their own words before any formal argument is introduced.

The deductive chain from the textbook is built step by step on the board: since ∠a + ∠b = 180° (linear pair) and ∠a + ∠d = 180° (linear pair on the other side), subtracting gives ∠b = ∠d. The class constructs the parallel argument for ∠a = ∠c. The textbook's phrasing — 'this is what we call a proof in mathematics' — is highlighted and discussed.

Figure it Out, section 5.1 p.107 ("Is it always true that vertically opposite angles are equal....") is worked in pairs: students write a short justification using only the linear-pair relationship, without measuring, for a general angle ∠a. Selected students read their justifications aloud for class critique.

Students write a two-sentence proof summary in their notebooks: the statement of the vertically opposite angles property and the one-line reason that derives it from linear pairs. Teacher checks for the logical connective — 'because' or 'therefore' — in each student's writing.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is writing '∠b = ∠d because they look equal' — insist that the written justification names the two linear-pair equations explicitly. Having established that vertically opposite angles are equal through this deductive chain, the class is well placed to recognise the same reasoning pattern in later sections.

periods.activity_title: Right-Angle Crossings and Lines That Never Meet

textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe Fig. 5.5 and describe how the various line segments meet using mathematical vocabulary (point, endpoint, midpoint, meet, intersect) and degree measures. Are line segments ST and UV likely to meet if extended?
Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel in Fig. 5.6 (dot grid with lines a through i)?
Are line segments OP and QR in Fig. 5.5 likely to meet if extended?

time_bands.activity: Students draw two intersecting lines and measure all four angles; when all read 90°, they mark the standard small square at the vertex. The definition is stated: perpendicular lines are those whose four intersection angles are all equal, each measuring 90°. Students identify perpendicular pairs in a simple classroom diagram.

Students examine Fig. 5.5 individually. Figure it Out, section 5.3 p.109 ("Observe Fig. 5.5 and describe how the various line segments meet....") is tackled in writing, with students required to use the vocabulary: intersect, endpoint, midpoint, perpendicular. Figure it Out, section 5.3 p.109 ("Are line segments OP and QR in Fig. 5.5 likely to meet if extended?") follows as a paired discussion.

The formal definition of parallel lines is introduced from the textbook: lines on the same plane that never meet however far extended. The teacher note on coplanarity is discussed briefly. Students examine Fig. 5.6 and answer Figure it Out, section 5.3 p.110 ("Which pairs of lines appear to be parallel...."), recording their pairs with reasons.

Whole-class share: student pairs defend their parallel-line choices from the dot-grid figure. The class settles on the distinction between lines that look roughly parallel and lines whose direction guarantees no meeting — reinforcing the definition over visual impression.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often argue that lines 'look parallel' by eye without justifying direction; press them to state why an extension would not meet. Watch for confusion between a line segment having an endpoint and a full line that continues indefinitely — Fig. 5.5 raises this directly.

textbook_segments.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines in Paper Folding

periods.activity_title: Folding Lines Into Existence: Parallel and Perpendicular

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fold a square sheet of paper horizontally in half multiple times; count parallel lines formed (pattern: 2ⁿ + 1 after n folds). Make a vertical fold and observe it is perpendicular to previous folds. Fold along a diagonal and find a parallel crease.

Fold a square sheet to make a centre crease, fold edges to centre, then fold top-right and bottom-left corners onto the crease to form triangles. Reason whether crease lines a, b, c are parallel to p, q, r respectively.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 5.11, mark parallel lines with arrow notation and perpendicular lines with a square symbol. (a) How did you spot the perpendicular lines? (b) How did you spot the parallel lines?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.4 p.114
homework.description: In Fig. 5.13, which line is parallel to line a — line b or line c? How do you decide?

time_bands.activity: Activity 2, p.111 ("Fold a square sheet of paper horizontally in half multiple times; count parallel lines formed....") is carried out in groups. After each fold, groups count crease lines and enter results in a table: 0 folds → 1 line, 1 fold → 3, 2 folds → 5, 3 folds → 9. Groups articulate the 2ⁿ + 1 pattern in their own words and then make a vertical fold, observing that the new crease meets every horizontal crease at 90°.

Activity 2 (corner folds), p.112 ("Fold a square sheet to make a centre crease, fold edges to centre, then fold top-right and bottom-left corners....") is carried out. Groups reason in writing whether crease lines a, b, c are parallel to p, q, r respectively, using the direction of each fold as their argument. Standard notation — arrow marks for parallel, square for perpendicular — is introduced and students mark their actual folded sheets.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.113 ("In Fig. 5.11, mark parallel lines with arrow notation and perpendicular lines with a square symbol....") is completed individually. Students answer parts (a) and (b) in writing, describing their identification strategy in a sentence each.

Quick whole-class check: teacher holds up a folded sheet and asks students to call out a parallel pair and a perpendicular pair. The pattern 2ⁿ + 1 is written on the board and students verify it matches their tables.

periods.teacher_notes: The 2ⁿ + 1 pattern surprises many students — let groups discover it before writing it on the board. A common slip in the corner-fold activity is assuming crease lines are parallel without reasoning about direction; ask groups to justify by describing what each fold preserves.
materials: square sheets of paper (one per student, extras for groups)

periods.activity_title: Eight Angles, Four Values: Reasoning About Transversals

textbook_items_in_class.description: Is it possible for all eight angles formed by a transversal crossing two lines to have different measurements? Why or why not?
What about five different angle measures — is that possible for the eight angles formed?

time_bands.activity: Students draw a transversal crossing two lines, label all eight angles 1–8, and measure each. They record their eight values and immediately notice pairs of equal angles. The definition of a transversal — a line intersecting two other lines — is read from the textbook, and students identify which of their angles are at the upper intersection and which at the lower.

Figure it Out, section 5.5 p.115 ("Is it possible for all eight angles formed by a transversal crossing two lines to have different measurements?") is posed for small-group debate. Groups apply the vertically opposite angles property (established for any intersection) to argue that angles 1 = ∠3, ∠2 = ∠4, ∠5 = ∠7, ∠6 = ∠8 — reducing eight values to at most four.

Figure it Out, section 5.5 p.115 ("What about five different angle measures — is that possible for the eight angles formed?") is tackled: groups reason that five distinct values would require one pair of vertically opposite angles to differ, which contradicts the established proof. Selected groups share their written reasoning for class critique.

Class agrees on the conclusion: the maximum number of distinct angle values among the eight is four. Students write this conclusion with a one-line justification in their notebooks, referencing vertically opposite angles by name.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who accept 'eight different angles are impossible' without stating why — the vertically opposite angles argument must be named explicitly. Encourage groups to frame their reasoning as 'if … then …' to begin developing the logical connective habits the proof-based sections ahead require.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw line l and transversal t intersecting at X with ∠a = 60°. Mark point Y on t and draw line m through Y at 60° to t (matching ∠a). Observe that l and m appear parallel; verify that corresponding angles are equal.

Given parallel lines l and m with transversal t (Fig. 5.19), trace ∠a on tracing paper and place it over ∠b to check that corresponding angles are equal. Verify all four corresponding angle pairs with a protractor.

Given non-parallel lines l and m (Fig. 5.20), attempt to draw a transversal t such that one pair of corresponding angles is equal. Observe that this is impossible, confirming the necessary condition for parallelism.

time_bands.activity: Activity 3, p.115-116 ("Draw line l and transversal t intersecting at X with ∠a = 60°. Mark point Y on t and draw line m through Y at 60°....") is carried out individually. Students observe that l and m appear to run side by side without meeting. The vocabulary 'corresponding angles' — same positional slot at each intersection — is introduced and the four corresponding pairs are named.

Activity 4, p.117 ("Given parallel lines l and m with transversal t (Fig. 5.19), trace ∠a on tracing paper and place it over ∠b....") uses tracing paper to superimpose angles. Students verify all four pairs and confirm equality with a protractor, recording results. Activity 5, p.117 ("Given non-parallel lines l and m (Fig. 5.20), attempt to draw a transversal t such that one pair of corresponding angles is equal....") follows: students discover that equal corresponding angles on non-parallel lines is impossible.

Class discussion synthesises the three activities into the biconditional: lines are parallel if and only if corresponding angles are equal. Teacher writes both directions ('if parallel then equal'; 'if equal then parallel') on the board and asks students to match each direction to one of the three activities they just did.
Students write the biconditional in their own words and sketch a labelled diagram showing one corresponding angle pair on parallel lines and one on non-parallel lines, marking the difference.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often accept only the forward direction ('parallel implies equal') and miss the converse; the contrast between Activities 4 and 5 is the pivot — make sure students state both directions before moving on. A common error is labelling non-corresponding angles (e.g., an alternate angle) as a corresponding pair because they 'look the same'; positional description (same corner at each intersection) corrects this.

periods.activity_title: Constructing Parallel Lines with Set Square and Paper Fold

textbook_items_in_class.description: Can you draw a line parallel to l that goes through point A (Fig. 5.23)? Describe your method using tools from your geometry box.
Why are lines l and m parallel to each other in the paper-folding construction of Fig. 5.24?

time_bands.activity: The set-square method is demonstrated: place the set square's right-angle corner on line l, draw a perpendicular, slide the set square to a new position along l, draw a second perpendicular. Students perform this construction twice — once from the teacher's demonstration, once independently. They label the two new lines and the baseline l, and name the corresponding angles (both 90°) that prove the new lines parallel.

The paper-folding method is carried out: fold to create a line t perpendicular to l through point A, then fold again to create line m perpendicular to t through A. Students label l, t, m and write a one-sentence explanation of why l ∥ m. Figure it Out, section 5.7 p.119-120 ("Why are lines l and m parallel to each other in the paper-folding construction of Fig. 5.24?") is answered in writing, citing corresponding angles.

Figure it Out, section 5.7 p.119 ("Can you draw a line parallel to l that goes through point A (Fig. 5.23)? Describe your method using tools from your geometry box.") is tackled individually. Students choose either the set-square or paper-folding method and write a step-by-step description in their own words, naming the angle relationship that guarantees parallelism.

Two students with different methods share their descriptions. Class identifies the common thread: in both methods a transversal creates equal corresponding angles of 90°, and that equality is the reason the lines are parallel.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes slide the set square without keeping one edge firmly on the baseline, which skews the second perpendicular; have them press the ruler firmly against the baseline while sliding. Having established that corresponding angles equal if and only if lines are parallel, the set-square construction's logic becomes transparent once students recognise the 90° angles as the corresponding-angle pair.

periods.activity_title: Alternate Angles: Proof and Multi-Step Reasoning

textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 5.25, if ∠f is 120°, find the measure of alternate angle ∠d by first finding corresponding angle ∠b of ∠f, then using the fact that ∠d is the vertically opposite angle of ∠b.
Parallel lines l and m intersected by transversal t. Given ∠6 = 135°, find all other 7 angles using corresponding angles (∠2, ∠4, ∠8 = 135°) and linear pairs (∠1, ∠3, ∠5, ∠7 = 45°).

Lines l and m intersected by transversal t. Given ∠a = 120° and ∠f = 70°. Determine whether l ∥ m by comparing corresponding angle ∠b (= 60°, since ∠a + ∠b = 180°) with ∠f (= 70°). Not equal, so not parallel.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.8 p.123
homework.description: Find the ten angles marked (a through j) in Fig. 5.30, which shows various transversal configurations with some angles given.

time_bands.activity: Activity 6, p.120 ("In Fig. 5.25, if ∠f is 120°, find the measure of alternate angle ∠d by first finding corresponding angle ∠b of ∠f, then using the fact that ∠d is the vertically opposite angle of ∠b....") is worked through as a class. The deductive chain — ∠f = ∠b (corresponding), ∠b = ∠d (vertically opposite), therefore ∠f = ∠d — is written on the board step by step, naming each rule. Interior angles summing to 180° are introduced as a third relationship.

Example 1, section 5.8 p.120-121 ("Parallel lines l and m intersected by transversal t. Given ∠6 = 135°, find all other 7 angles....") is read and then reconstructed by students without the book. Students write each step in a chain, naming the rule: corresponding, linear pair, vertically opposite. Errors are corrected against the textbook solution.

Example 2, section 5.8 p.121 ("Lines l and m intersected by transversal t. Given ∠a = 120° and ∠f = 70°. Determine whether l ∥ m....") is attempted individually. Students write the comparison: ∠b = 180° − 120° = 60° ≠ 70° = ∠f, therefore not parallel. Pairs check each other's reasoning and flag any step that skips the rule-name.

Class consolidates the three relationships — corresponding angles, alternate angles, interior angles — with a reference table drawn by students in their notebooks: name, positional description, and the condition under which they are equal (or sum to 180°).

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in multi-step chains is applying a rule without stating which angle is the 'given' and which is 'found' — insist that each step names both angles and the rule connecting them. Example 3, section 5.8 p.121-122 (interior angle sum) and Example 4, section 5.8 p.122 (parallelogram figure) are recommended as self-study for students who want to see the rules applied in more complex configurations.

periods.activity_title: Angle Chains in Context and the Illusion of Parallelism

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.8 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angle represented by a in each of four sub-figures in Fig. 5.31 involving parallel lines and transversals.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.8 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 5.34, AB ∥ CD ∥ EF and EA ⊥ AB. If ∠BEF = 55°, find x and y.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.8 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find ∠NOP in Fig. 5.35, where ∠LMN = 40°, ∠MNO = 96°, ∠OPQ = 52°. [Hint: draw lines parallel to LM and PQ through N and O.]

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.8 p.124 ("Find the angle represented by a in each of four sub-figures in Fig. 5.31 involving parallel lines and transversals....") is worked in pairs. Each pair completes all four sub-figures and writes a one-line rule-name beside each computed value. Pairs then exchange books to check whether the rule-names match the calculations.

Figure it Out Q5, section 5.8 p.125 ("In Fig. 5.34, AB ∥ CD ∥ EF and EA ⊥ AB. If ∠BEF = 55°, find x and y....") and Figure it Out Q6, section 5.8 p.125 ("Find ∠NOP in Fig. 5.35, where ∠LMN = 40°, ∠MNO = 96°, ∠OPQ = 52°....") are attempted individually. The hint in Q6 — draw auxiliary parallel lines through N and O — is a key strategic move; students who are stuck are prompted with the question 'What extra line would help you apply the rules you know?'

Section 5.9 is engaged: teacher shows the parallel-illusion images from the textbook and students write a brief response to the reflective prompt — what causes the lines to appear non-parallel? Discussion brings out the idea that surrounding patterns distort visual judgment, and that geometric measurement and reasoning, not appearance, settles the question.
Students name the one rule they found most powerful across the angle-computation exercises today and write it as a single sentence — a personal close to the chapter's applied work.

periods.teacher_notes: Q6's auxiliary-line strategy is the hardest move in the chapter; validate any student who draws the auxiliary lines even if the subsequent calculation has an error, since the strategic insight is the harder part. Section 5.9 carries no exercises and no formal content — keep the reflection genuinely open so students articulate the distinction between visual perception and geometric proof in their own words.
materials: textbook (open to Fig. 5.31, Fig. 5.34, Fig. 5.35, and section 5.9 illusion images)

items.prompt: Two straight lines intersect at a point, forming four angles. One of the four angles measures 65°. What are the measures of the other three angles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angle opposite the 65° angle is also 65° (vertically opposite angles are equal). Each adjacent angle forms a linear pair with the 65° angle, so each measures 180° − 65° = 115°. The three remaining angles are 65°, 115°, and 115°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the linear-pair sum (180°) to find the two adjacent angles and the vertically-opposite-angles property to find the fourth.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes all four angles at an intersection are equal, ignoring the linear-pair relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly finds the two linear-pair angles but invents a fourth value (130°) rather than applying vertically opposite angles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly identifies the two 115° angles but assigns 130° instead of 65° to the vertically opposite angle, suggesting a doubling error.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to sketch the intersection and label the known angle, then use the linear-pair rule one step at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a general expression for all four angles when one angle is x°, then verify it works for any value of x.

exercise.description: In Fig. 5.2, if ∠a is 120°, figure out the measurements of ∠b, ∠c, and ∠d without drawing and measuring them.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes perpendicular lines?

options.label: A
options.text: Two lines that never meet, however far they are extended

options.label: B
options.text: Two lines that intersect so that all four angles formed are equal, each measuring 90°

options.label: C
options.text: Two lines that intersect so that two of the four angles are 90° and the other two are 180°

options.label: D
options.text: Two lines on the same plane that meet at exactly one point at any angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Perpendicular lines intersect so that all four angles formed are equal, each measuring 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition: perpendicular lines are the special case of intersection where every angle at the crossing equals 90°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses perpendicular lines with parallel lines.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student knows that right angles are involved but incorrectly believes two angles are 90° and two are 180°, misapplying the linear-pair sum.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student identifies that the lines meet at one point — true of all intersecting lines — but omits the 90° condition that defines perpendicularity.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the definition in section 5.2 and sketch the intersection with the small square symbol before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one real-world example of perpendicular lines and explain in their own words why the 90° condition matters.

exercise.description: Observe Fig. 5.5 and describe how the various line segments meet using mathematical vocabulary (point, endpoint, midpoint, meet, intersect) and degree measures. Are line segments ST and UV likely to meet if extended?

items.prompt: A transversal crosses two lines, forming eight angles in total. What is the maximum number of angles among these eight that can have different measurements?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The maximum is 4. At each intersection, the two pairs of vertically opposite angles must be equal, reducing 8 angles to at most 4 distinct values.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the vertically-opposite-angles property at each of the two intersections: each pair must be equal, so at most 4 distinct values are possible.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not applied the vertically-opposite-angles property and treats all eight angles as independent.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student partially reduces the count — perhaps applying the property at only one intersection — but does not complete the argument at both.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-applies a constraint, perhaps believing all angles at one intersection must equal all at the other, yielding only 2 distinct values.

inclusivity.support: Have the student draw the figure, label angles 1–8, and circle the vertically opposite pairs at each intersection before counting distinct values.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to describe exactly what configuration of two lines and a transversal would achieve exactly 4 distinct angle values, and what would give fewer.

exercise.description: Is it possible for all eight angles formed by a transversal crossing two lines to have different measurements? Why or why not?

items.prompt: In the parallel illusions shown in section 5.9, lines that are actually parallel appear to be slanted or bent. Name one reason, discussed in the chapter, why geometric reasoning is more reliable than visual impression for deciding whether lines are parallel.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Surrounding patterns can distort our visual judgment, making parallel lines look non-parallel. Geometric reasoning — using measurement or angle properties — does not depend on appearances and therefore gives a reliable answer.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the chapter's contrast between visual perception (which surrounding context can distort) and geometric proof or measurement (which is independent of visual context).

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the illusion images in section 5.9 and the chapter's note about measurement versus appearance before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to describe in their own words one geometric test — using angles or measurement — that could confirm two lines are truly parallel, regardless of how they look.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.8 p.124
exercise.description: Find the angle represented by a in each of four sub-figures in Fig. 5.31 involving parallel lines and transversals.

items.prompt: Two lines intersect at a point, forming angles p, q, r, and s in order around the intersection. Using only the fact that a straight line forms a 180° angle, explain why p must equal r.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Angles p and q form a linear pair, so p + q = 180°. Angles q and r also form a linear pair, so q + r = 180°. Since both expressions equal 180°, we get p + q = q + r, and subtracting q from both sides gives p = r.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Chain two linear-pair equations (p + q = 180° and q + r = 180°) and subtract to derive p = r without any measurement.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student write the two linear-pair equations first, then look for a common term to subtract.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the same argument for any angle value — using a letter instead of a number — to show the result holds generally.

exercise.description: Is it always true that vertically opposite angles are equal for any pair of intersecting lines? Check for different measures of ∠a and reason whether the property holds generally.

items.prompt: A student claims that the eight angles formed when a transversal cuts two lines can include exactly five different angle measures. Explain why this claim is incorrect.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: At each of the two intersections, the vertically opposite angles must be equal (proved from linear pairs). This forces the four angles at one intersection to contain at most two distinct values, and likewise at the other. So the eight angles together have at most four distinct values — never five.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the vertically-opposite-angles property at each intersection to show that the maximum number of distinct values across all eight angles is four, ruling out five.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw the figure, mark which pairs must be equal by the vertically-opposite-angles property, then count how many free values remain.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to describe a configuration that achieves exactly three distinct angle measures and explain what relationship between the two lines produces it.

exercise.description: What about five different angle measures — is that possible for the eight angles formed?

items.prompt: A transversal crosses two lines. At the upper intersection the angle in the top-right position measures 72°. At the lower intersection the angle in the top-right position also measures 72°. Explain, using the corresponding-angles result established in section 5.6, whether the two lines must be parallel. Then state what would happen to this conclusion if the lower angle were 75° instead.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two angles described are corresponding angles — they occupy the same positional slot (top-right) at each intersection. Section 5.6 establishes that lines are parallel if and only if corresponding angles are equal. Since both measure 72°, the lines must be parallel. If the lower angle were 75° instead, the corresponding angles would be unequal (72° ≠ 75°), so the lines would not be parallel.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the biconditional from section 5.6: corresponding angles equal if and only if the lines are parallel, then test the altered value against the same criterion.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to re-read both directions of the biconditional ('if parallel then equal' and 'if equal then parallel') before writing their answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain what would change in the construction of Activity 3 (section 5.6) if the second angle were drawn at 75° rather than matching the first.

exercise.description: Draw line l and transversal t intersecting at X with ∠a = 60°. Mark point Y on t and draw line m through Y at 60° to t (matching ∠a). Observe that l and m appear parallel; verify that corresponding angles are equal.

items.prompt: Parallel lines l and m are cut by transversal t. Angle ∠f at the lower intersection measures 110°. Using the chain of reasoning in section 5.8 — corresponding angles and vertically opposite angles — explain why the alternate angle ∠d at the upper intersection also measures 110°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Since l and m are parallel, corresponding angles are equal, so the corresponding angle ∠b of ∠f at the upper intersection also measures 110°. Angle ∠d is vertically opposite to ∠b at that same intersection, so ∠d = ∠b = 110°. Therefore the alternate angle ∠d equals ∠f.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Chain: ∠f = ∠b (corresponding angles, lines parallel) and ∠b = ∠d (vertically opposite), so ∠f = ∠d.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student write the two steps separately — first name the corresponding angle, then name the vertically opposite angle — before connecting them.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to prove the same result using interior angles (∠f + ∠d = 180° is wrong for alternate angles — challenge them to spot the error in that approach and explain why).

exercise.description: Parallel lines l and m intersected by transversal t. Given ∠6 = 135°, find all other 7 angles using corresponding angles (∠2, ∠4, ∠8 = 135°) and linear pairs (∠1, ∠3, ∠5, ∠7 = 45°).

items.section_title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines in Paper Folding
items.prompt: A square sheet of paper is folded horizontally in half three times, producing a set of equally spaced horizontal crease lines. One more fold is then made vertically. How many crease lines are now visible in total on the unfolded sheet? How many of these are perpendicular to the horizontal creases? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three horizontal folds produce 2³ + 1 = 9 horizontal crease lines. One vertical fold produces 1 vertical crease line. Total crease lines = 9 + 1 = 10. The vertical crease is perpendicular to every horizontal crease, so exactly 1 crease line is perpendicular to the horizontal set (or equivalently, 9 horizontal lines are perpendicular to the 1 vertical line).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the 2ⁿ + 1 pattern for n horizontal folds (n = 3 gives 9 lines), add the 1 vertical crease, and identify the vertical as perpendicular to all horizontal lines.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student build a table for 1 fold, 2 folds, 3 folds before using the formula, then add the vertical crease separately.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to calculate the total for n horizontal folds and 1 vertical fold, expressing the total and the number of perpendicular pairs as expressions in n.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.113
exercise.description: In Fig. 5.11, mark parallel lines with arrow notation and perpendicular lines with a square symbol. (a) How did you spot the perpendicular lines? (b) How did you spot the parallel lines?

items.prompt: A student wants to draw a line through point P that is parallel to a given line l. She places a set square so that one of its sides lies along l, then slides the set square along a ruler until the same side passes through P, and draws the line. Explain, using the corresponding-angles criterion, why the line she draws is guaranteed to be parallel to l.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The ruler acts as a transversal. When the set square's right-angle side rests on l, the angle between that side and the ruler is 90°. When the set square is slid so the same side passes through P, the angle between the new line and the ruler is still 90°. The two 90° angles are corresponding angles with respect to the transversal (ruler). Since corresponding angles are equal, the new line is parallel to l.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the ruler as the transversal, recognise the two 90° angles as corresponding angles, and invoke the corresponding-angles criterion for parallelism.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to label the ruler as the transversal and the two 90° angles in a sketch, then state the corresponding-angles rule in one sentence.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain whether the method would still work if the set square were tilted at 60° instead of 90°, and why.

exercise.description: Can you draw a line parallel to l that goes through point A (Fig. 5.23)? Describe your method using tools from your geometry box.

items.prompt: In a figure, parallel lines p and q are cut by transversal t. The angle on the left side of t above line p measures 48°. Find: (a) the angle on the right side of t above line p, (b) the alternate angle to the 48° angle (on the right side of t, below line q), and (c) the interior angle between the parallel lines on the same side as the 48° angle. Show each step with the rule used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The angle on the right side of t above p forms a linear pair with 48°, so it measures 180° − 48° = 132°. (b) The alternate angle to 48° is on the right side of t below q; alternate angles are equal when lines are parallel, so it measures 48°. (c) The interior angle on the same side as 48° is between p and q on the left of t; it is the corresponding angle of 132° (which equals 132°) OR equivalently, interior angles on the same side sum to 180°, so it measures 180° − 48° = 132°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply linear pair (for part a), alternate-angles equality (for part b), and interior-angle sum of 180° or corresponding angles (for part c) in sequence.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw and label the figure first, identify which angle is 'alternate' and which is 'interior' by position, then apply one rule at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify part (c) using two different methods — the interior-angle sum rule and the corresponding-angles rule — and confirm they give the same answer.

exercise.description: Find the angle represented by a in each of four sub-figures in Fig. 5.31 involving parallel lines and transversals.
